To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) distributional similarity is a powerful tool for extracting facts from unstructured texts, and (2) the iterative application of distributional similarity can be used to bootstrap a high coverage fact extractor from a few seed facts.

(i) distributional similarities can be exploited for the iterative acquisition of extraction patterns, (ii) distributional similarities are a useful tool for ranking and validation of candidate facts, and (iii) distributional similarity is the only feature required to achieve high coverage and quality in the extraction of facts from Web documents.

(a) distributional similarities between names are a powerful source of information that can be used to extract facts from unstructured Web documents; (b) the iterative acquisition of extraction patterns from a small number of seed facts can lead to a high coverage of the Web; and (c) the combination of extraction patterns and distributional similarities can lead to a very high precision of the extracted facts.
In summary, our research is concerned with

1) the extraction of a large set of facts from unstructed text, 2) the use of distributional similarity for fact validation and ranking, and 3) the integration of distributional similarities into the acquisition of contextual extraction patterns.
